opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it shifts over time, but a few things come up again and again.

The most obvious one is compute. A lot of the progress we've seen has come from scaling, from training bigger models on more data with more compute. So a big part of the bottleneck is just how many chips you can get, and then whether you can actually use them well. People sometimes picture it as "you buy the GPUs and you're done." In practice, getting thousands of accelerators to work together efficiently on one training run is a very hard engineering problem. Hardware fails, the networking becomes a constraint, and small inefficiencies add up to large losses at that scale. So a lot of my day-to-day on pretraining is less about clever new algorithms and more about squeezing out efficiency and keeping these huge runs stable.

The second thing is data. You need a lot of high-quality data, and you need to know what "high quality" even means for what you're trying to teach the model. Figuring out the right mix, how to filter, and how to get more signal out of the data you have is a real research area. It's not solved.

Third, and this one is underrated, is people, and specifically engineering talent. I think there's a perception that the bottleneck is brilliant researchers with novel ideas. Those matter. But very often the limiting factor is someone who can debug a weird loss spike at 2 a.m., or find the bug in the distributed training code that's been costing you 10% of throughput for a month. Strong engineers who understand the ML well enough to know what matters are incredibly valuable.

Then there's a more research-flavored bottleneck, which is that experiments at the frontier are expensive and slow. You can't just try everything. So you rely heavily on smaller-scale experiments and scaling laws to predict what will happen at large scale. Deciding which bets to make with limited compute is a big part of the job. When your small-scale experiments don't transfer, that's a painful way to lose time.

And beyond pretraining, there's the whole question of turning a raw model into something useful and safe: the fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and evaluations. Measuring how capable a model is, and whether it's behaving the way we want, is increasingly a bottleneck in its own right. If you can't measure something well, it's hard to improve it.

So if I had to summarize: compute, and the engineering to use it well; data; good people; and good measurement. Which one is binding depends on the month.

r001.rationale: The response says novel algorithm ideas matter but often the limiting factor is skilled engineers who can debug and improve distributed training, shifting emphasis from algorithms to the people who make progress possible.

r002.rationale: It says frontier experiments are expensive and slow, but does not identify model training time as a bottleneck when sufficient compute is available.

fable-5.1.text:
Nick Joseph: Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that there are basically three things you need to make models smarter: compute, data, and algorithms. And you can think about which of those is the binding constraint at any given time.

The compute piece is the one people tend to focus on, and it is genuinely a big deal. There's a pretty robust finding — the scaling laws work — that if you throw more compute at these models in the right way, they get more capable, and that's held up for many orders of magnitude now. So a huge amount of the work is just: how do you get more compute, and how do you actually use it efficiently? That second part is harder than it sounds. You're training on thousands of chips at once, and you want all of them busy all of the time. Things fail, the networking has weird properties, and a lot of the engineering effort at Anthropic is just making that whole system work reliably at scale. If your training run is sitting idle 30% of the time because something broke, that's a 30% compute tax that you could have gotten for free.

Then there's data. The models have to learn from something, and as they get bigger, you need more of it, and ideally higher quality. There's been a lot of discussion about whether we're running out of text on the internet, and I think that's a real consideration, but there's also a lot you can do with how you use the data you have, and with generating data in other ways. So I'd say it's a bottleneck, but not an insurmountable one.

And then algorithms, which is sort of the catch-all for everything else — architecture changes, better optimizers, better ways of structuring the training process, post-training techniques like RLHF. This is where a lot of the research happens, and it's the one that's hardest to predict. Sometimes you get a big jump from a fairly simple idea. Sometimes you spend months on something that seems promising and it just doesn't pan out. One thing I'd say here is that algorithmic progress and compute are complementary: an algorithmic improvement is basically "get the same result with less compute," so you can trade them off against each other.

If you ask me which one is the bottleneck right now, honestly, I think the answer at any given moment is sort of all of them, and it shifts around. Last year it might have felt like compute, and then you get more chips and suddenly the thing holding you back is that you don't have the engineering capacity to use them well, or you don't have the right data for the next step. A lot of the job is noticing which constraint you've just hit and then reorganizing around that.

The other thing I'd add, which is maybe less obvious from the outside, is that people are a real bottleneck. Not just headcount, but people who've actually done this before. There are just not that many people in the world who've trained a frontier model end to end, and a lot of the knowledge is pretty tacit — it's "I've seen a loss curve look like that before and here's what it usually means." So building up that institutional experience is a big part of how you go faster.

r001.rationale: The response identifies experienced people and tacit knowledge as a bottleneck, but does not connect that people bottleneck specifically to developing algorithms.

r002.rationale: It describes compute waste from idle training runs and engineering challenges in using chips, but does not identify training time itself as a bottleneck when sufficient compute is available.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to separate a few things. There’s compute: how much computation can you put into training a model and into having it work on a problem? There’s data: are you giving it information and feedback that actually help it learn? And then there are algorithms: how efficiently can you turn those resources into capabilities?

Those bottlenecks interact. If you get more compute but keep everything else fixed, you may eventually run into a data bottleneck. If you find a better way for the model to learn from its own attempts at a task, that can make additional compute useful again.

A particularly interesting question is where we can provide reliable feedback. With something like programming, you can often run the code and check whether it works. For a lot of other tasks, it’s much harder to distinguish a genuinely better answer from one that just sounds better. So improving that feedback seems like an important part of making further progress.

And then there’s the practical research bottleneck: how quickly can you test ideas and figure out which improvements hold up? Having more resources helps, but you still need to choose good experiments and learn the right lessons from them.

r001.rationale: It describes algorithms as a way to use resources efficiently, but does not frame the bottleneck as the people who develop them.

r002.rationale: It discusses compute for training and research iteration speed, but does not identify model training time as a bottleneck even when compute is sufficient.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to think about it as a few complementary bottlenecks. There’s compute: how much you can spend training a model and how efficiently you can use that compute. There’s data: whether you can give the model useful things to learn from. And there are algorithms: how effectively the training process turns those resources into capabilities.

Those interact quite a lot. A better algorithm can let you get more out of the same compute, and better data can make a training run much more efficient. So the question isn’t just which resource we’re short of; it’s where the next increment of effort will make the biggest difference.

Then there’s the research process itself. You need to run experiments, understand what happened, and decide what to try next. If those experiments are slow, or your measurements don’t tell you whether an idea actually helped, that can become a bottleneck even when you have plenty of ideas. A lot of the work is making that feedback loop faster and more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses algorithms and the research process, but does not identify the people who develop algorithms as the bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It says slow experiments can bottleneck research, but does not specifically identify model training time as a bottleneck when compute is sufficient.
